summary:
Kenya criminalises consensual sex between men under the colonial-era Penal Code, with imprisonment of up to 14 years, and the provision applies regardless of the nationality of those involved. There is no statute governing gender identity and no codified pathway for legal gender recognition, although intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender.

Police conduct is the most immediate risk for a trans visitor. Twenty-six trans and intersex interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi described routine detention on pretexts such as being drunk and disorderly, followed by on-the-spot extortion, including demands to "look for 5,000 shillings". Several of those interviewed use traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through public space safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

Document access is obstructed in practice. Evidence placed before the High Court showed that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused corrections by civil registration offices, with some spending close to four years' wages on attempts that failed.

Violence against sexual and gender minorities is documented rather than alleged. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's Lives on the Line report, published in September 2025, covers October 2023 to September 2024, was built with more than 14 community organisations, and expressly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16/2019 that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence.

The courts have moved in the opposite direction from the police. On 12 August 2025 the Eldoret High Court found that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections for transgender Kenyans and directed the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act; the petition was brought by a trans Kenyan subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered gender determination while incarcerated. On 20 May 2026 the Milimani High Court in Nairobi, in a decision delivered by Justice Bahati Mwamuye in Petition 27 of 2020, ruled on the constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The Mombasa Court of Appeal had held forced anal testing unconstitutional in 2018, with compensation awarded in 2024, and the Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration in 2023. A man was sentenced to 50 years' imprisonment in December 2024 for killing an LGBTQ activist.
tangentialFactors:
LGBTI civil-society groups may operate in Kenya, but only within a restrictive civic space, according to the UK Home Office country policy note of February 2025. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's data collection relied on purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision, and those organisations continue to raise awareness and provide community spaces despite the documented violence.

Societal discrimination is long-standing and reaches beyond legal exposure. The US State Department human rights report for the 2010 reporting year recorded widespread discrimination based on sexual orientation causing loss of employment and education, and noted that in February 2010 religious leaders in Mtwapa demanded the closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute, a demand bearing on access to health services for men who have sex with men. The same report recorded that the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya was permitted to register and operate.

Kenya's trajectory over the past decade has been court-driven rather than legislative: judicial decisions have struck down forced anal testing and affirmed freedom of association, while the legislature has produced no framework for gender recognition. The Constitution's Article 27 and Article 28 guarantees of equality and dignity sit alongside a criminal statute that has not been repealed.
localsOnly:
Kenyan residents live under the same criminal provisions as visitors, and the absence of a codified legal framework for gender recognition applies to them directly: civil registration offices refuse marker corrections in the overwhelming majority of cases, and the courts have yet to see that practice translated into a statutory process.

The Eldoret High Court's 12 August 2025 judgment addresses conditions that fall on residents in state custody. The petition established that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections for transgender detainees, and that the petitioner had been subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and a court-ordered gender determination during incarceration.

Community infrastructure exists and is documented. The Lives on the Line report was produced with more than 14 community organisations, and active LGBTIQ+ organisations provide both awareness work and physical community space. A petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination has been filed; its outcome is not recorded in the sources available here.

Intersex Kenyans hold a distinct legal position, recognised as a third gender, which does not extend to transgender or gender-diverse people seeking marker change.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Transgender Protection Rights Act directed by the Eldoret High Court on 12 August 2025 has been drafted, introduced or enacted is unresolved in the sources available here.

The operative remedy of the Milimani High Court decision of 20 May 2026 is not specified in the inventory: the sources confirm that the court ruled on the constitutional right to legal gender recognition but do not state what relief was granted or whether a statutory recognition process was ordered.

No sourced material in this inventory records prosecutions of the criminal provisions against foreign nationals or visitors, so the practical likelihood of charge rather than extortion cannot be assessed from these sources.

The outcome of the petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination is unresolved.

The US State Department human rights report used here covers the 2010 reporting year and describes conditions more than a decade old; it is retained only as evidence of the long-standing pattern of societal discrimination and of the registration status of LGBTQ organisations at that time.

The inventory does not state whether the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16/2019 has been appealed, varied or remains binding notwithstanding the Kenya Human Rights Commission's challenge to it.
